newsitem.title: USA: US carmakers get their way, 110 seen as dlr/yen cap.
newsitem.headline: US carmakers get their way, 110 seen as dlr/yen cap.

text.p: Though the White House showed little sympathy last June to U.S. automaker gripes over the rising dollar, currency players say they are taking no chances and will pointedly shun the dollar whenever it nears 110 yen.
U.S. officials never deviated from their canned calls for a "strong" dollar, but the car companies' persistence raised red flags for investors putting their portfolios on the line.
"You could sort of tell there was some sensitivity in a lot of people's minds," said Tom Dickson, a currency fund portfolio manager at Franklin/Templeton Group.
"It sort of sets an area (110 yen per dollar) where, if we keep coming back up to those levels, it would be a good area to add yen to currency portfolios," he said.

The dollar peaked at 111.19 yen on July 8 after beginning the year below 104. Repeated massive purchases of dollars by Japanese monetary authorities helped guide the U.S. unit higher, analysts maintained.

In response, Big Three auto officials made repeated trips to Washington and gave several press interviews complaining that the rising dollar was hindering their efforts to gain market share in Japan by making their exports more expensive.
Even skeptics concede the ruckus dimmed the prospect for futher dollar gains versus the yen.
"It has appeared for quite some time that these complaints are not being listened to," said Michael Faust, foreign exchange manager at money manager Bailard Biehl and Kaiser in San Mateo, Calif.
"But it does represent a drag on the dollar and anytime you get above 110, it will definitely resurface," he added.
Auto officials said the government gave them no commitment to rein in the dollar. The Bank of Japan has slashed dollar purchases of late, but that likely reflects mere coincidence.

"Perhaps all that pressure helped out a bit, not that the U.S. government took action, but it may have helped persuade the Japanese government to (reduce) its buying of dollars," said Van Bussmann, corporate economist at Chrysler Corp.
"We had no inkling anybody at (the U.S.) Treasury was in contact with the Bank of Japan," he added.
In fact, Bank of Japan figures show a sharp decline in reserve asset growth in the second quarter of 1996.
Japan's reserves, mainly dollars, but also other foreign currencies and gold, rose by 2.6 trillion yen in 1994, 5.4 trillion yen in 1995 and 2.32 trillion yen in the first quarter of 1996 alone.
But that growth slipped to 755 billion yen in the second quarter of 1996 as the dollar made its first assault on 110 yen in over two years.

Yet any attempt to link Big Three grumbling with a drop in reserve growth would be pure fantasy, said Arthur Alexander, president of the Japan Economic Institute of America, a think tank partially funded by the Japanese government.

"What we're seeing is the beginning of the end of the Japanese policy of supporting the dollar by enormous purchases of dollars for yen," Alexander said. "I don't think the (U.S.) auto industry had any effect."

A prolonged Japanese economic slump has allowed the BoJ to flood the market with yen without fear of sparking domestic inflation. But as the economy crawls out of its current malaise, inflation will limit Japan's will to support the greenback, Alexander said.
"Right now Japan doesn't have to worry about inflation, but in six months they'll have to," he added.
Investors noted the current U.S. presidential election campaign provides a fitting backdrop for potential White House concessions on foreign exchange policy to the automakers.
The temptation to placate Detroit and reinforce the economy's considerable momentum as the November 5 election day draws near would seem hard to resist, investors said.
"A lot of people are going to believe the administration will be sympathetic to automaker demands," Faust said. "I've been surprised at how unsympathetic they've been."
To their credit, U.S. officials led by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin seem to have accepted their limited ability to dictate the value of the dollar, analysts said.
Rubin, a one-time currency maven at Goldman, Sachs and Co, has shrewdly persuaded market players the White House wants the dollar to remain firm without specifying a target level.

"He's been very careful not to give the market the impression the dollar's current level is ever a problem," Faust said. "When the market sees indecisiveness, it's not taken well and we really haven't seen that this time around."
